title: Combined migrator powers (unstakeFor + onlyOwnerOrMigrator on withdrawRewardToken) yield a single-key drain of all NFTs and all phUSD, contrary to the migration plan
description:
The migration plan's 'NFTStakerV2 deltas' section enumerates exactly two surgical additions: `stakeFor(beneficiary, amount)` and `withdrawRewardToken(to, amount) external onlyOwner`. The implementation deviates from the plan in three reinforcing ways that, together, hand the migrator role full control of the staker's economic surface:

1. **unstakeFor exists at all and routes principal to the migrator.** `unstakeFor(beneficiary, amount)` (lines 543-562) is gated by `onlyMigrator` and `whenNotPaused`, but performs no check that the position it is unstaking was originally deposited via `stakeFor`. The `users[beneficiary]` ledger co-mingles positions created by `stake(amount)` (direct staker) and `stakeFor(beneficiary, amount)` (migrator-deposited). The only precondition is `users[beneficiary].amount >= amount` (line 547). Crucially, line 558 — `stakedToken.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, stakedId, amount, "")` — transfers the ERC1155 principal to `msg.sender` (the migrator), not to the beneficiary. The migrator can therefore enumerate any address with a non-zero stake (via Staked/StakedFor events and the public `users(address)` getter) and call `unstakeFor(victim, users[victim].amount)` to pull the victim's NFTs into the migrator's own wallet. Pending phUSD is correctly routed to the beneficiary by `_safePay(beneficiary, pending)` on line 552, but the principal is gone. The function is not mentioned anywhere in the plan; the documented migration is one-way (V1.unstake by users, V2.stakeFor by helper).

2. **withdrawRewardToken access is widened from plan-spec onlyOwner to onlyOwnerOrMigrator.** The plan (NFTStakerV2 deltas section, code block on line 188) explicitly specifies `withdrawRewardToken(address to, uint256 amount) external onlyOwner`. The implementation uses `onlyOwnerOrMigrator` (line 564), letting the migrator address drain the full phUSD balance to an arbitrary recipient `to` once `totalStaked == 0 && paused()` hold. The plan models the helper as a stateless single-purpose contract that 'has no admin, no upgrade path. Holds no funds between txs.' Granting it (or any future migrator) drain rights is a deviation from the documented authorisation surface.

3. **The two powers compose.** The migrator can: (a) call `unstakeFor(beneficiary_i, users[beneficiary_i].amount)` for each known beneficiary until `totalStaked == 0` — NFTs land at the migrator, each beneficiary's pending phUSD is paid to them but the bulk of the reward budget is not yet paid out; (b) with totalStaked == 0, cooperate with pauser (or be pauser) to call `pause()`; (c) call `withdrawRewardToken(migratorAddr, fullBalance)` to drain the remaining phUSD. End state: migrator holds every id-6 NFT that was deposited and the residual phUSD reward budget. The plan models the migrator as orchestrating only the deposit direction of a one-way migration; the implementation gives the same role the ability to undo every deposit AND sweep the reward pool.

Code references:
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:521-541` — `stakeFor` creates positions credited to `users[beneficiary]` with no migrator-association marker.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:458-483` — `stake` writes to `users[msg.sender]`, indistinguishable in storage from `stakeFor`-created positions.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:543-562` — `unstakeFor`, transfers principal to `msg.sender` (migrator) on line 558.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:564-578` — `withdrawRewardToken`, `onlyOwnerOrMigrator`, sweeps to arbitrary `to`.
impact:
All NFT principal held in the staker plus the full phUSD reward budget are at the discretion of a single migrator address. For the documented migration (~139 id-4 NFTs converted to id-6 plus a runway-matching phUSD mint on the order of thousands of phUSD), a migrator that goes off-design or is repurposed can drain every NFT and the full reward pool in one transaction sequence — without invoking owner, without invoking pauser (if it is also pauser or if pauser cooperates), and only briefly invoking the pause window. Beneficiaries are left with the small in-flight pending paid during step (a) of the drain and stale `users[B_i]` entries with zero amount.

The constraint that `totalStaked == 0 && paused()` must hold for the phUSD sweep gates the timing window but not the magnitude. `unstakeFor` itself has no `paused()` precondition, so step (a) can be performed at any time while the contract is operating normally.

Note: the migrator is owner-set and revocable, so a malicious owner argument falls under the project's accepted centralisation envelope. This finding focuses on the structural code defects: (i) the user's principal ledger and the migrator's withdrawal capability are not separated, and (ii) the documented onlyOwner → implemented onlyOwnerOrMigrator deviation expands the trust surface beyond the plan. Under the plan's deployment (migrator = stateless MigrationHelper), the attack is structurally impossible — the risk is that the contract authorises a much wider set of actions than the plan's helper actually uses, so any deviation from the planned helper expands risk dramatically.
recommendation:
Apply three reinforcing changes that collectively collapse the trust surface back to what the plan describes:

1. **Remove `unstakeFor` (and the `UnstakedFor` event) entirely.** It is not required by the migration plan and beneficiaries can use the standard `unstake` path themselves. Alternative if the function must stay: route the NFT transfer to the beneficiary (`stakedToken.safeTransferFrom(address(this), beneficiary, ...)`) instead of `msg.sender`, eliminating the principal-redirection vector; or tag positions at creation with a migrator-deposited flag and constrain `unstakeFor` to only operate on that subset.

2. **Revert `withdrawRewardToken` to plan-spec `onlyOwner`.** Remove the `onlyOwnerOrMigrator` path. If migrator drain access is genuinely needed, update the plan to document the operational rationale and consider scoping the migrator's allowed `to` parameter to `owner()` only — so the migrator can trigger the sweep but cannot redirect funds.

3. **Document the migrator's intended trust model explicitly on-chain.** (See DEDUP-05.)

With those three changes, the migrator's only power is the documented `stakeFor` — which itself doesn't transfer beneficiary funds out of the staker.
attack_scenario:
1. Owner deploys NFTStakerV2, funds runway with R phUSD (per plan step 11), sets `targetAPY = 0.3e18`, sets `migrator = MigrationHelper` per step 9.
2. Users migrate via `migrationHelper.migrateAndStake(amount)`; helper calls `staker.stakeFor(user, amount)`. Over time N id-6 NFTs accumulate in the staker; users' `users[B_i].amount` reflect their deposits.
3. (Several months later, post-migration window.) A future incident requires rotating the helper. Owner calls `setMigrator(newHelper)` in good faith — `newHelper` is a future contract written for a follow-up incident, or an EOA, or a multisig. If `newHelper` is buggy, compromised, or operationally repurposed:
   a. For each known beneficiary `B_i` (enumerable from Staked/StakedFor events): `newHelper.unstakeFor(B_i, users[B_i].amount)`. NFTs aggregate at `newHelper`. Each `B_i` receives only their small in-flight pending phUSD.
   b. After all unstakes, `totalStaked == 0`. `newHelper` (or cooperative pauser) calls `pause()`.
   c. `newHelper.withdrawRewardToken(newHelper, rewardToken.balanceOf(staker))`. All phUSD lands at `newHelper`.
4. End state: `newHelper` holds every staked id-6 NFT plus the residual phUSD budget. Honest beneficiaries hold only the small pending paid during step (a) and stale `users[B_i]` entries with zero amount. No on-chain recourse.

This is the unintended-privilege framing: the plan never authorised the migrator to hold this combination of powers, so an honest owner could grant the role in good faith to a helper later found to be misbehaving. The current deployed migrator (MigrationHelper, stateless, single-purpose) does not exhibit this behaviour — the concern is the role's powers as encoded in the staker, not the current role-holder.
